quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "The rebranding project was important, but with the product launch coming up, leadership decided to deal with it later."
quests.hint: It's about deliberately delaying something, not cancelling it.
quests.explanation: 'On the back burner' means a task is set aside for later, though not forgotten entirely. "We're putting the office redesign on the back burner until next quarter."
quests.origin: A literal kitchen image: a pot moved to a rear stove burner still cooks, just more slowly and with less attention than one at the front.

quests.instruction: Manager: 'Any updates on new features?' Developer: 'A few big ones are ___, but nothing's ready to announce yet.'
quests.hint: It means something is currently being developed or planned, not finished.
quests.explanation: 'In the pipeline' means something is in progress or being planned, though not yet finished. "There are three new hires in the pipeline for next month."
quests.origin: From industrial pipelines, where material moves steadily from one stage to another before reaching its final destination.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches this situation: "After months of waiting for approval, the design team was finally told they could officially begin building the app."
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Receive official approval to begin or proceed with something.
quests.explanation: 'Get the green light' means to receive permission or approval to proceed. "We finally got the green light to launch the new product."
quests.origin: From traffic lights, where green signals it's safe and permitted to go.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Fail to achieve the intended goal or result.
quests.explanation: 'Miss the mark' means to fail to meet a target or expectation. "The ad campaign missed the mark with younger audiences."
quests.origin: From archery, where an arrow that doesn't hit the target, or 'mark,' has failed its purpose.

quests.instruction: When the CEO showed up to the meeting in shorts and flip-flops, it definitely ___ among the board members.
quests.hint: It means causing surprise or mild disapproval through an unusual action.
quests.explanation: 'Raise eyebrows' means to cause surprise, suspicion, or disapproval. "Her sudden resignation raised eyebrows across the department."
quests.origin: A literal description of the facial expression people make — eyebrows lifting — when surprised or skeptical.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches this situation: "After the client finally signed the contract, the team immediately started every process needed to begin the project."
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Start a process that will lead to further developments.
quests.explanation: 'Put the wheels in motion' means to start a process moving forward. "Once we had the budget, we put the wheels in motion for the new office."
quests.origin: A mechanical image: once a vehicle's wheels begin turning, the whole machine is set into motion.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "The venue was booked, the catering was arranged, but nobody remembered to send the invitations — the whole event nearly fell apart."
quests.hint: It's about failing at a responsibility you were supposed to handle.
quests.explanation: 'Drop the ball' means to fail to do something you were responsible for. "I dropped the ball on confirming the flight times."
quests.origin: From ball sports, where literally dropping a catchable ball is a simple, visible failure of duty.

quests.instruction: Client: 'Let me know as soon as there's any update on the shipment.' Team: 'Of course, we'll ___.'
quests.hint: It means regularly updating someone with new information.
quests.explanation: 'Keep someone posted' means to continue informing them of developments. "I'll keep you posted once we hear back from the supplier."
quests.origin: From the older sense of 'post' as mailing or displaying notices — 'posted' meant kept informed through regular updates.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Continue all the way to the end of a difficult task, without giving up.
quests.explanation: 'Go the distance' means to persist through an entire difficult task or challenge to completion. "Training for months, she was determined to go the distance in the marathon."
quests.origin: From boxing, where a fighter who 'goes the distance' lasts every scheduled round without being knocked out.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Not yet decided; uncertain.
quests.explanation: 'Up in the air' means something is undecided or uncertain. "Our vacation plans are still up in the air until we hear about time off."
quests.origin: A literal image of something tossed upward, not yet landed or settled — used figuratively since the 1700s.

quests.instruction: Colleague: 'It's been a while since we discussed the budget.' You: 'Let's ___ sometime this week to go over the numbers.'
quests.hint: It means to make brief contact with someone to check in or share a quick update.
quests.explanation: 'Touch base' means to make brief contact with someone, often to check in. "I'll touch base with the vendor before Friday."
quests.origin: From baseball, where a runner must touch each base in sequence — checking in briefly at each point before moving on.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches this situation: "With the funding delayed, the company decided to pause the new office expansion until next year."
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Temporarily stop or delay something.
quests.explanation: 'Put something on hold' means to pause or delay it temporarily. "We had to put the renovation on hold until permits came through."
quests.origin: From telephone 'hold' — a call paused but not disconnected, waiting to resume.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "When the projector broke five minutes before her presentation, she improvised a whiteboard sketch and kept the talk going smoothly."
quests.hint: It's about reacting quickly and cleverly to an unexpected problem.
quests.explanation: 'Think on your feet' means to react quickly and effectively to unexpected situations. "Great customer service reps have to think on their feet."
quests.origin: A literal image of thinking while standing, ready to act, rather than sitting and deliberating slowly.

quests.instruction: When she heard her flight had been moved up two hours, she had to ___ and rush to the airport.
quests.hint: It means stopping all other activities immediately to deal with something urgent.
quests.explanation: 'Drop everything' means to immediately stop all other activity to deal with something urgent. "When the client called in a panic, he dropped everything to help."
quests.origin: A literal, direct image of physically abandoning whatever is in your hands to attend to something more pressing.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Monitor or track someone or something closely.
quests.explanation: 'Keep tabs on' means to watch or monitor closely. "The manager keeps tabs on inventory levels every week."
quests.origin: Likely from 'tab' meaning a running account or record, tracked and checked regularly, dating to late 1800s American slang.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "Instead of raising the issue with his direct supervisor, he emailed the department director directly, skipping the usual chain."
quests.hint: It's about bypassing the person you'd normally report to.
quests.explanation: 'Go over someone's head' means to bypass a person's authority by appealing to someone higher up. "She went over her manager's head and complained directly to HR."
quests.origin: A literal spatial image of reaching upward, past the person directly in front of you, to someone positioned higher.

quests.instruction: With the original project manager on leave, one of the junior designers decided to ___ and organize the team.
quests.hint: It means stepping forward to direct or be responsible for something.
quests.explanation: 'Take the lead' means to assume a position of leadership or direction. "No one volunteered, so she took the lead on the presentation."
quests.origin: From racing, where the runner or horse 'in the lead' is ahead of the others, guiding the pace.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches this situation: "With so many new students enrolling, one quiet kid who was struggling never got noticed by any of his teachers all semester."
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Be overlooked or neglected, usually because of a poorly organized system.
quests.explanation: 'Fall through the cracks' means to be overlooked, often due to a flawed system. "His application fell through the cracks during the office move."
quests.origin: A literal image of something small slipping through gaps in flooring or infrastructure, unnoticed until it's too late.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Use personal influence or connections to get an advantage.
quests.explanation: 'Pull strings' means to use private influence or connections to get something done. "He pulled some strings to get us a table at the fully booked restaurant."
quests.origin: From puppetry, where a puppeteer controls a puppet's movements invisibly, from behind the scenes, by pulling strings.

quests.instruction: Nervous parent: 'Are you sure the kids will be okay with the new babysitter?' Friend: 'Don't worry, they're ___.'
quests.hint: It means someone or something is being taken care of by a capable, trustworthy person.
quests.explanation: 'In good hands' means being cared for by someone competent and reliable. "Leave the negotiations to her — you're in good hands."
quests.origin: A literal, reassuring image of being physically held securely, extended to being entrusted responsibly to someone.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches this situation: "The chef used to get every dish right without thinking, but lately even his simplest recipes keep coming out wrong."
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Lose a skill you once had, especially one that used to come easily.
quests.explanation: 'Lose your touch' means to lose a skill or ability you previously had naturally. "He used to close every deal, but lately he seems to have lost his touch."
quests.origin: Uses 'touch' in the sense of a skilled hand or ability, a usage present in English since at least the 1600s.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "When no one else volunteered to lead the crisis response, the newest team member offered to take charge."
quests.hint: It's about accepting a challenge or responsibility, especially when others hesitate.
quests.explanation: 'Step up to the plate' means to take responsibility for a difficult task, especially voluntarily. "When the manager quit suddenly, she stepped up to the plate."
quests.origin: From baseball, where a batter steps up to home plate, ready to take their turn and face the pitch.

quests.instruction: Before submitting the grant application, the team double-checked every requirement to ___ in case reviewers looked closely.
quests.hint: It means preparing thoroughly for all possible outcomes or problems.
quests.explanation: 'Cover your bases' means to prepare thoroughly for all possibilities. "We covered our bases by getting three separate quotes before deciding."
quests.origin: Also from baseball, where defensive players must cover, or protect, every base to prevent runners from advancing.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Be the person in control, making all the important decisions.
quests.explanation: 'Run the show' means to be in charge and control how things are done. "Officially she's a co-founder, but everyone knows she runs the show."
quests.origin: From theatre production, where the person 'running the show' controls the cues, timing, and overall performance.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Perform several different roles or jobs, often within a small team.
quests.explanation: 'Wear many hats' means to take on multiple roles or responsibilities. "At a small startup, you end up wearing many hats."
quests.origin: A literal image of switching hats to represent switching jobs, each hat symbolizing a different role.

quests.instruction: Team lead: 'Everyone needs to ___ on this project — we can't have anyone coasting while others do the heavy lifting.'
quests.hint: It means doing your fair share of work within a group.
quests.explanation: 'Pull your weight' means to do your fair share of the work in a group effort. "Everyone on the team needs to pull their weight before the deadline."
quests.origin: From rowing, where each rower must pull their oar with full effort, matching their fair share relative to their own body weight.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Present arguments and reasons in support of an idea or decision.
quests.explanation: 'Make a case for' means to argue in favor of something with supporting reasons. "She made a strong case for switching suppliers."
quests.origin: A legal metaphor: lawyers 'make a case' by building an argument supported by evidence, extended to everyday persuasion.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "The podcast was awkward for the first few episodes, but by episode ten, the hosts had found a natural rhythm and were doing their best work."
quests.hint: It's about reaching a comfortable, effective, and consistent rhythm after an adjustment period.
quests.explanation: 'Hit its stride' means to reach a smooth, effective rhythm after a period of adjustment. "The new restaurant struggled at first, but it's really hit its stride now."
quests.origin: From running, where a runner 'finds their stride' once their pace becomes steady and efficient.

quests.instruction: After a rough first year with heavy losses, the business finally started turning a profit — everyone agreed they had ___.
quests.hint: It means reaching a turning point where a difficult situation starts to improve.
quests.explanation: 'Turn the corner' means to pass a critical point after which a situation starts improving. "After weeks of illness, he finally turned the corner and started feeling better."
quests.origin: A literal image of walking around a street corner, moving from one path onto a new, more favorable one.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Returning to regular, often tiring, everyday work after a break.
quests.explanation: 'Back to the grind' means returning to routine, often tedious, work after time off. "Vacation's over — back to the grind tomorrow."
quests.origin: From 'grind' meaning hard, repetitive labor, an image traceable to the tedious work of literally grinding grain.
